title: Service Entry Sheet Invoicing: Why Services Suppliers Cannot Bill Like Goods Suppliers
summary: Services invoices fail AP portals because the service entry sheet must be approved first. How SES-based billing works and how to automate it line by line.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:** A service entry sheet is the services equivalent of a goods receipt: a record of work actually delivered that the buyer must approve *before* an invoice can clear. Goods suppliers match PO to receipt to invoice. Services suppliers must match PO to approved entry sheet to invoice, and the approved quantity often differs from the planned one — which is why services invoices are rejected far more frequently. The approval itself stays human, but entry sheet creation, line-by-line PO mapping, document attachment and status tracking are all mechanical and automatable.


Ask an AR team that bills services why their invoices get rejected and you will not hear about tax codes or layout rules. You will hear about the entry sheet. Something was delivered, somebody has to confirm it, and until that confirmation exists the invoice has nowhere to attach itself.


This is the structural difference between selling goods and selling work, and it is almost completely absent from the discussion of invoice delivery automation. Guidance on AP portals assumes a goods transaction: a purchase order, a delivery, a receipt, an invoice. Services suppliers live in a different sequence with an extra gate in the middle — and that gate is where their cash gets stuck.


## What Is a Service Entry Sheet?


A service entry sheet is a record of services actually performed against a purchase order line, submitted to the buyer for approval before invoicing. In SAP environments it is a formal document type; in[SAP’s own S/4HANA documentation](https://help.sap.com/docs/SAP_S4HANA_ON-PREMISE) it sits in the procurement flow between the PO and the invoice. Other systems call it a service sheet, a work confirmation, a timesheet approval or a service receipt. The mechanics are the same wherever it appears.


The purpose is to answer a question that goods procurement answers trivially and services procurement cannot: did this actually happen, and how much of it? When a pallet arrives at a warehouse, someone counts it. When a maintenance crew spends three days on site, or a staffing agency supplies eleven contractors for a fortnight, there is nothing to count at a loading bay. The entry sheet is the substitute — a claim of what was delivered, which an operational manager either confirms or adjusts.


That distinction matters because it changes who approves. A goods receipt is confirmed by warehouse staff following a procedure. An entry sheet is confirmed by the manager who actually oversaw the work, against their own memory and records. That person does not work in finance, does not care about your DSO, and did not have approving your entry sheet on their plan for the week.


## How Does Services Billing Differ From Goods Billing?


The sequences look similar and behave completely differently.


Stage Goods supplier Services supplier


Authorisation Quantity PO with fixed line items Services PO, often a limit or blanket PO with a value ceiling


Delivery proof Goods receipt, confirmed on arrival Service entry sheet, confirmed by an operational manager


Who confirms Warehouse or receiving team, procedurally Operations or site manager, from judgement and records


Typical confirmation lag Hours to days Days to weeks


Evidence required Delivery note Timesheets, visit reports, site logs, signed job sheets


Match for invoicing PO to receipt to invoice PO to **approved** entry sheet to invoice


Common failure Quantity or price variance Invoicing planned quantity instead of approved quantity


The three-way match that AP teams run is well understood, and we cover the mechanics of it in our guide to[AI agents and three-way matching for purchase order reconciliation](https://peakflo.co/blog/ai-agents-three-way-matching-purchase-order-reconciliation-guide) . Services billing effectively inserts a prior match: the entry sheet must first be reconciled against the PO line and approved, and only then can the invoice be reconciled against the entry sheet.


Two consequences follow, and both land on the supplier.


**The approval lag sits before invoicing, not after.** A goods supplier invoices on dispatch and waits for payment terms to run. A services supplier waits for an entry sheet approval they do not control, and only then starts the payment clock. That is why services suppliers routinely carry structurally higher DSO than goods suppliers on identical contractual terms — a dynamic closely related to the[invoice delivery gap that quietly consumes working capital](https://peakflo.co/blog/invoice-delivery-gap-working-capital-dso-reduction) .


**The approved quantity becomes the only billable quantity.** This is the detail that generates most services rejections. A supplier plans 40 hours, delivers 40 hours, and the manager approves 38 because two were spent on something they consider out of scope. If the invoice says 40, it fails. The resolution is not a tax correction or a resubmission with a different reference — it is a commercial conversation about those two hours, which can take weeks.


## Why Do Services Invoices Fail in AP Portals?


Portals enforce the entry sheet relationship mechanically, and the failure messages rarely explain what went wrong.


**Invoicing ahead of approval.** The entry sheet is submitted but not yet approved, and the invoice has nothing to match. Some portals reject outright; others accept the invoice and park it silently, which is worse, because the AR team believes it is submitted and waits.


**Billing the planned quantity.** Described above. Mechanically detected, commercially resolved, slow either way.


**Mapping to the wrong PO line.** A services PO may carry many lines — different rates, different scopes, different remaining balances. Services delivered under line 4 and billed against line 2 will fail even though the total is correct. Our post on[exception management and tolerance rules](https://peakflo.co/blog/invoice-exception-management-automation-tolerance-rules) explains why a correct total does not survive a line-level check.


**Missing supporting documents.** The buyer requires timesheets or a signed visit report, the requirement lives in the contract rather than the portal interface, and nobody on the current AR team knows about it. This is the failure mode that most rewards institutional memory and most punishes staff turnover.


**Exceeding the PO limit.** On a limit PO, cumulative entry sheets eventually hit the ceiling and submissions block automatically. Suppliers typically discover this at the moment they most need to bill, because nobody was tracking the remaining balance after each submission.


**Period mismatch.** Work delivered across a month boundary, billed in one period, approved against another. Common in facilities and maintenance contracts with rolling schedules.


Rejection cause Detected by Time to resolve Preventable before submission?


Invoice ahead of entry sheet approval Portal, mechanically Days Yes — poll approval status first


Planned rather than approved quantity Portal, mechanically Weeks, needs commercial agreement Yes — bill from the approved sheet


Wrong PO line mapping Portal, mechanically Days Yes — map at line level


Missing supporting documents Buyer’s approver, manually Days to weeks Yes — attach per buyer rule set


PO limit exceeded Portal, as a hard block Weeks, needs a PO increase Yes — track remaining balance


Period mismatch Buyer’s approver or portal Days Partly — align billing to approval periods


The pattern worth noticing: nearly every cause is preventable before submission. These are not judgement failures. They are bookkeeping failures that occur because the information needed to prevent them is scattered across a PO in the buyer’s portal, a timesheet system, an ERP and somebody’s memory.


## Which Suppliers Are Most Affected?


Any supplier billing work rather than shipped goods, which is a larger population than the phrase “services procurement” suggests.


Engineering, maintenance and MRO contractors bill labour hours and parts against long-running POs with site-level approvers. Facilities management bills recurring scheduled work where the entry sheet is effectively a monthly attendance record. Staffing and professional services bill timesheets, and the entry sheet *is* the timesheet, approved by the hiring manager rather than by procurement. Logistics and freight handling bill per movement or handling event, often with accessorial charges that need separate substantiation. IT services bill a mix of fixed retainer and variable consumption, where only the variable part needs an entry sheet. Construction subcontracting bills progress against work packages with retention and certification layered on top.


What they share is that the person approving the work is operational, not financial — and that the supporting evidence lives in a system the buyer cannot see. Staffing suppliers in particular face the compounding problem we describe in[invoice delivery for staffing agencies, where the source of truth is a timesheet system rather than an ERP](https://peakflo.co/blog/staffing-agency-invoice-delivery-client-portals-automation) .


## What Can Actually Be Automated When Approval Stays Human?


This is where services suppliers often conclude, wrongly, that automation cannot help them. The reasoning goes: our bottleneck is the buyer’s manager approving the entry sheet, we cannot automate that, therefore there is nothing to gain.


The approval is indeed human and should stay that way. But the approval is a small fraction of the elapsed time. Everything surrounding it is mechanical.


**Entry sheet creation and line mapping.** Reading delivered quantities from a timesheet or job system, finding the right open PO line in the buyer’s portal, and mapping line by line. Purely mechanical, and the step where wrong-line errors originate.


**Document attachment.** Pulling the timesheet, visit report or delivery order and attaching it according to that buyer’s rule set. Mechanical, and the step most dependent on tribal knowledge today.


**Pre-submission variance checks.** Comparing quantity, rate and tax against the PO line before anything is submitted, so a mismatch surfaces as an internal exception rather than a buyer rejection weeks later. This is the same preventive logic described in[real-time invoice validation with instant error feedback](https://peakflo.co/blog/real-time-invoice-validation-vendor-error-feedback) .


**Approval status polling.** Checking whether the entry sheet has been approved, and with what quantities. Today this is a person logging into a portal to look — the exact repetitive work that fills an AR team’s week, as described in[why AR teams lose hours to customer portal hell](https://peakflo.co/blog/manual-invoice-delivery-customer-portal-automation) .


**Invoicing the approved quantities.** Once approved, generating and submitting the invoice against the approved numbers rather than the planned ones. Mechanical, and it eliminates the single largest rejection category.


**Balance tracking and escalation.** Updating remaining PO value after each submission and flagging an approaching limit early enough to request an increase before billing stops.


Step Mechanical or judgement Automatable What it prevents


Create entry sheet, map PO lines Mechanical Yes Wrong-line rejections


Attach supporting documents Mechanical Yes Approver stalls on missing evidence


Pre-submission variance check Mechanical Yes Mechanical rejections entirely


**Approve the entry sheet** **Judgement** **No — stays with the buyer** —


Invoice approved quantities Mechanical Yes Planned-vs-approved mismatches


Poll status, track PO balance Mechanical Yes Silent parking, hard blocks


Because entry sheets are created and approved inside the buyer’s own portal, the practical route in is the interface itself rather than an integration. That is what an[AI browser agent](https://peakflo.co/blog/what-is-an-ai-browser-agent-finance-back-office-guide) is for: it works the portal the way your AR analyst does, which means no buyer-side IT project and no waiting in an integration queue — the constraint that makes[every new client portal a revenue bottleneck](https://peakflo.co/blog/new-client-portal-onboarding-velocity-invoice-automation) .


Structured e-invoicing does not remove this gate. Standards such as the[Peppol BIS Billing specification](https://docs.peppol.eu/poacc/billing/3.0/) and the European[eInvoicing framework](https://ec.europa.eu/digital-building-blocks/sites/display/DIGITAL/eInvoicing) standardise the invoice document, which is genuinely useful. The entry sheet approval still happens in the buyer’s system, on the buyer’s timeline. Professional bodies including[CIPS](https://www.cips.org/) and the[Institute for Supply Management](https://www.ismworld.org/) treat work confirmation as a control objective rather than a formatting problem, and that framing is the correct one.


## How Should a Services Supplier Measure This?


Four numbers make the problem visible, and most services AR teams track none of them.


**Entry-sheet-to-approval days** , separated from invoice-to-payment days. Reporting a single DSO figure hides the fact that much of the delay occurs before an invoice exists. Splitting them usually reveals that the pre-invoice phase is the larger half.


**Approved-versus-submitted quantity variance** , by customer. A customer that consistently approves 95% of submitted hours has a scoping problem worth a commercial conversation, not a billing problem worth a resubmission.


**Rejection rate by cause** , using the taxonomy above. Mechanical causes should trend to near zero once checks move pre-submission; if they do not, the checks are not actually running.


**PO balance headroom** , as days of billing remaining before the limit blocks submissions. This converts a surprise into a schedule.

## Our Verdict


Services suppliers are not worse at billing than goods suppliers. They are playing a different game with an extra approval gate, and most invoice delivery tooling was designed for the game without that gate.


Our position: treat the service entry sheet as the primary billing artefact and the invoice as a derived document. Teams that invoice from their own plan and then reconcile to the approved sheet afterwards will keep generating rejections indefinitely, because the plan and the approval disagree often enough to matter. Teams that invert the order — submit the entry sheet, wait, then invoice exactly what was approved — eliminate most mechanical rejections outright.


Accept that the approval stays human and automate everything around it. The approval is rarely the largest component of elapsed time; the waiting, the checking, the re-keying and the rework are. Measure entry-sheet-to-approval separately from invoice-to-payment, and the size of the opportunity becomes obvious immediately.


## Conclusion


The service entry sheet is the reason services billing feels harder than it should, and it is not going away. It exists because work that leaves no physical trace still needs confirming, and that confirmation legitimately belongs to the person who oversaw the work.


What does not need to be manual is everything else: creating the entry sheet, mapping it to the right PO line, attaching the evidence, catching variances before submission, polling for approval and billing the approved quantities. Fix that sequence and services billing stops being structurally disadvantaged — the approval gate remains, but it stops being surrounded by a week of avoidable work.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is a service entry sheet?


A service entry sheet is a record of services actually delivered against a purchase order line, submitted for the buyer’s approval before invoicing. It functions as the services equivalent of a goods receipt, confirming that work happened and in what quantity.


### Why do services invoices get rejected more often than goods invoices?


Because services billing has an extra approval gate. A goods invoice matches a PO and a goods receipt. A services invoice must match a PO and an approved entry sheet, and the approved quantity frequently differs from the quantity the supplier planned to bill.


### What is the difference between a service entry sheet and a goods receipt?


A goods receipt is confirmed by a warehouse against a physical delivery. An entry sheet is confirmed by an operational manager against work that leaves no physical trace, which makes it slower, more subjective and more dependent on supporting evidence.


### What is a limit purchase order in services procurement?


A limit or blanket PO authorises spending up to a ceiling without specifying exact quantities in advance. Suppliers bill against it progressively via entry sheets, and submissions are blocked automatically once cumulative value reaches the limit.


### Can an AI browser agent submit service entry sheets?


Yes. Because entry sheet creation happens in the buyer’s portal interface, an AI browser agent can create the entry sheet, map lines to the open PO, attach supporting documents and capture the confirmation without any buyer-side integration.


### Why does invoicing the planned quantity cause rejections?


Because the buyer approves the entry sheet, not the plan. If a manager approves 38 hours against a planned 40, an invoice for 40 fails the match. The invoice must follow the approved entry sheet quantities exactly.


### What supporting documents do service entry sheets need?


Typically timesheets, visit or site reports, delivery orders, inspection records or signed job sheets. The specific list varies by buyer and is usually defined in the contract rather than shown in the portal interface.


### How long does service entry sheet approval take?


Commonly several days to a few weeks, because approval depends on an operational manager rather than a finance process. This delay sits entirely before invoicing begins, which is why services suppliers carry structurally higher DSO.


### Which industries rely most on service entry sheet invoicing?


Engineering and maintenance contractors, facilities management, staffing and professional services, logistics and freight handling, IT services, and construction subcontracting. Any supplier billing labour or recurring work rather than shipped goods.


### Can services billing be automated if approvals are manual?


Yes. The approval stays human, but entry sheet creation, line mapping, document attachment, status polling and invoicing the approved quantities are all mechanical and automatable, which removes most of the elapsed time.


### What happens when a services PO runs out of value mid-period?


The portal blocks further entry sheets or invoices until the buyer increases the PO. Tracking the remaining balance after every submission lets you request an increase before billing stops rather than after.


### Does Peppol or e-invoicing solve service entry sheet problems?


Only partly. Structured e-invoicing standardises the invoice document, but the entry sheet approval still happens in the buyer’s own system. The approval gate remains regardless of how the final invoice is transmitted.
